Hello, and thank you for joining us today. Last time we worked on finding evidence against your "not cut out" story, and you decided to record yourself saying a supportive script tonight. Did you manage to find some time to try that exercise before our appointment?

Also, since we didn't finish reviewing everything from last session, could we quickly take a minute to decide which topic brings you the most relief today—the anxiety about training camp, or perhaps refining that recording plan?

Yeah, I did try the recording thing last night. It was... weird, hearing my own voice like that. But I guess I could see how it might help if I keep at it.

I think I'd rather focus on the training camp anxiety today. That's been eating at me more than anything else lately. Every time I think about getting back on the track with the team, my stomach just drops.

Hearing your own voice sound so different from your inner critic must have been surprising, and it’s completely normal to feel a mix of curiosity and discomfort when listening to that contrast. Since you’re ready to tackle the training camp anxiety, let’s explore what that “stomach dropping” sensation is trying to protect you from right now. When you imagine being back on the track, is there a specific moment or outcome you’re fearing most—like making a mistake in front of everyone—or is it more about the pressure of performing perfectly?

It's definitely the fear of messing up in front of everyone. I keep replaying that fall in my head, and I just picture myself doing it again, but this time with the whole team watching. They'll see I'm not the same rider I used to be, and they'll just write me off as someone who can't handle the pressure anymore.

That image of falling in front of the entire team while feeling exposed is incredibly painful, and it makes total sense why your stomach would drop so hard. It seems like your brain is trying to prevent you from entering that situation entirely by convincing you that the worst-case scenario is inevitable. When you picture yourself making that mistake publicly, does the thought immediately spiral into believing that *everyone* will judge you harshly, or does it stay focused mostly on your own shame?

I think it starts with my own shame, honestly. Like I'm letting myself down more than anyone else. But then it does spiral—I start thinking about how the guys on the team will look at me differently, like I'm damaged goods or something. And once that thought sets in, I can't shake the feeling that I've already lost their respect, even before I've gotten back on the bike.

That spiral from personal shame to feeling permanently damaged by others' judgment is a very common pattern, and it explains why the fear feels so overwhelming. It seems like your brain has learned that protecting itself means assuming the worst outcome is guaranteed. If you paused for just one second to separate the prediction ("they will write me off") from the reality of the situation, what would be the first piece of factual evidence you could use to challenge that assumption? Have you ever seen another athlete struggle early on and still earn their place on the team?

Well... yeah, actually. There's this guy, Marcus, on the team. Last season he crashed hard during a practice run, and it took him weeks to get back to full speed. I remember some guys were skeptical at first, but by the end of the season he was leading our relay races again. I guess I forgot about that until now.

That example of Marcus is perfect proof that setbacks don't permanently disqualify athletes, yet your brain filtered him out because he succeeded despite the crash. It shows you have access to real-world evidence that contradicts your "damaged goods" story. If we imagined a script where you described Marcus's journey but added a line acknowledging that *he* faced the same internal doubt you do right now, would that make the difference between "he recovered" and "we can recover too"? How does that slight tweak change the meaning of his story for you?

Huh. When you put it that way, it does change things. I never really thought about what was going on inside Marcus's head during that time. I just saw him get back on the bike and succeed, but I didn't consider the doubt he probably felt too. Saying "we can recover too" instead of "he recovered" makes it feel... less like I'm alone in this. Like it's not just me being weak, it's part of the process.

That is such a profound insight, recognizing that Marcus wasn't just physically resilient but mentally navigating the same doubts you face right now. By shifting the narrative from "he survived" to "we survive together," you've turned his story into a roadmap for your own recovery rather than a distant event. Does framing it as a shared human experience—"us recovering"—make the fear of isolation slightly less intense for you right now?

Yeah, it does. I think the hardest part has been feeling like I'm the only one who's ever felt this way, like I'm broken in a way other athletes aren't. But knowing Marcus went through something similar and came out the other side... it makes me feel like maybe I can too. It's still scary, don't get me wrong, but at least I don't feel so alone in it anymore.

That connection to Marcus is powerful because it transforms your isolation into a shared challenge, proving that your struggle isn't unique to you. Since you found that reframing helpful, could we try applying it directly to your upcoming training camp? Imagine telling yourself, "Just like Marcus doubted himself after crashing, I will trust my ability to bounce back even if I stumble." Would speaking that line to yourself before heading out feel manageable, or does the idea of trusting your resilience still feel risky?

It feels... manageable, I think. Saying it out loud feels different than just thinking it. Like if I actually speak those words, there's no taking them back. But I guess that's the point, right? I need to commit to believing it, not just entertain the idea. I'll try saying that to myself before camp. Even if it feels awkward at first.

That commitment to speaking the words—even when they feel awkward—is exactly what turns a fleeting thought into a lasting tool. Since you've practiced this script with Marcus's story, does adding your own name to that sentence ("Just like Marcus doubted himself... **I** will trust my ability...") make it feel personally grounded enough to say right before camp? Or does the prospect of committing to that belief still feel like a big leap?

Adding my own name makes it feel more real, but also more... heavy, you know? Like now I'm actually responsible for following through with it. But I think that's a good kind of heavy. It's not the weight of failure I've been carrying around—it's the weight of a promise to myself. I think I can carry that.

That distinction between the weight of failure and the weight of a promise is crucial—it shifts the burden from something you must escape to something you choose to uphold. Since you feel capable of carrying that responsibility, let's finalize the plan for tonight. Could you record yourself saying, "Just like Marcus doubted himself after crashing, I will trust my ability to bounce back," right before you sleep? And if the words feel stiff at first, please just note that it takes practice to smooth them out, okay?

Yeah, I can do that. I'll record it tonight before bed, even if it feels a bit stiff at first. I think hearing it back a few times might help it sink in more. Thanks for pushing me on this—I wasn't sure I'd get to a place where I could actually commit to saying something like that to myself.

That courage to commit to the words, even when they feel unfamiliar, is a massive milestone in rebuilding your confidence. Please remember that the stiffness you feel tonight is just muscle memory adjusting to a new habit, not a sign that the words aren't working. 

Before we wrap up, could you share a quick word on how our session went so far? Was walking through Marcus's story and crafting that new promise helpful for you, or was there a part you felt we missed?

It was really helpful, actually. I came in here feeling like I was stuck in that spiral, and I'm leaving with something concrete I can actually do tonight. The Marcus thing opened my eyes—I'd been so focused on my own failure that I forgot other people go through this too. I think the only thing we might have missed is... how do I handle it if the recording doesn't work right away? Like if I say it and still feel anxious the next day?

That is such a thoughtful observation—you're already anticipating the possibility of setbacks, which shows incredible foresight. A great way to handle that is to treat the recording as a starting point, not a final verdict. If you listen and still feel anxious, simply remind yourself: "The fact that I spoke the words proves I chose hope over fear, even if my stomach hasn't settled yet." We can also add a backup plan for tomorrow morning, like taking three deep breaths before checking your phone, to reset the mood before the day gets harder. Does adding that safety net make you feel more confident about tackling the recording tonight?

Yeah, that actually helps a lot. Knowing I don't have to get it perfect the first time takes some of the pressure off. I like the idea of the deep breaths in the morning too—it gives me something small to do before my brain can start spiraling again. I think I'm ready to try this tonight.

That willingness to embrace imperfection and trust in small, manageable steps is exactly what builds lasting resilience. Remember, the goal isn't to eliminate the anxiety overnight, but to create a bridge between your old fears and your new choices. I'm proud of how far we've come today, turning a paralyzing spiral into a clear path forward. Is there anything else on your mind before we officially close this session?

Hello, and welcome back. To kick off our session, I'd like to briefly check in on how you've been feeling this week and then review what we worked on last time regarding your history exam. After that, we can set a fresh agenda for today based on what matters most to you. Could you share a bit about your recent mood and whether you were able to try that two-minute pause exercise we planned?

Hi. Uh, this week has been pretty rough, honestly. I tried the two-minute pause a couple times, but my mind just kept racing back to that F and how I'm probably going to fail the next test too. I couldn't really calm down.

When the panic spikes, it can feel like the brain overrides whatever calm technique we agreed on, leaving you stuck in that cycle again. Did you notice anything different in your body during those attempts compared to when you expected things to go wrong, or did the same physical symptoms return instantly?

Yeah, pretty much instantly. My chest gets tight, my stomach drops, and I start thinking, "See? This proves I'm a failure. I can't even do this simple exercise right." It's like my whole body just gives up before I even really start.

That immediate spiral of self-criticism ("this proves I'm a failure") suggests your brain interpreted the discomfort as confirmation of your worst predictions rather than just temporary anxiety. It sounds like the panic attacked harder the moment you realized you weren't perfectly successful with the exercise. Did you find yourself getting up to leave the room again during those failed attempts, or did you manage to stay seated despite the urge?

I actually got up and walked away both times. I told myself I'd come back to it later, but I never did. It's like my brain makes up this story that I'm just not cut out for History, or for anything really, and that's that. So why bother, you know?

That escape route makes total sense given how intense the shame felt when you couldn't control your own breathing. Your brain seems to be using the failed attempt as definitive proof of your "Failure" identity, convincing you that the effort wasn't worth it because the result was messy. Before we figure out how to interrupt that loop, I need to understand: when you walk away after that realization, what is the very first thought that pops into your head to justify leaving?
It's always, "I'll just fail anyway, so what's the point?" That thought comes before I even realize I'm standing up. It's like my body already knows the answer before my head catches up.

That pre-meditated decision to leave confirms how deeply rooted that "why bother" belief is—it acts as an autopilot mode for your avoidance. It sounds like your brain is trying to protect you from the pain of realizing you can't fix this on your own right now. Yeah, I can do that. One minute. I'll tell myself it's just static, just noise, and I don't have to act on it right away. I'll try that tomorrow after school.

No, that sounds fair. One minute with a timer, treating the panic like static, and then I'll just see what happens. I think I can manage that. Thanks.

You have shown tremendous resilience by sticking with this experiment despite the initial setbacks. I hope the "static" metaphor helps you navigate tonight, and please know I am here to listen whatever you discover when we speak again. Take care!

Oh, well... I'd say I'm around a 4 or 5 today. Not the worst, but definitely not great. I had to work a double shift at the restaurant yesterday, and I kept noticing how much quicker the younger waitresses were with their tables.

A four or five is honest reporting, and I appreciate you sharing that reality without sugarcoating it. Given that the initial plan wasn’t quite enough to hold the feeling, how would you rate your confidence right now in sticking with the new strategy tonight? I think my confidence is maybe a 3 out of 10 right now. I want to believe it could work, but part of me feels like I'm just fooling myself with these little tricks. But I'll try anything at this point, honestly. What three words did you have in mind?

I suggest focusing on three simple truths: "Kindness counts," "Effort matters," and "You are enough." These aren't complex arguments, but short anchors designed to bypass your logical defense mechanisms and speak directly to your core belief.

Before we lock this in, does framing it as a "quick reset" rather than a long speech feel less intimidating to you? And would you be okay if we scheduled this specifically for 10 minutes before your next shift starts, leaving the rest of the night free from pressure?

Those three phrases... they feel almost too simple, you know? Like my brain wants to argue with them. But I guess that's the point, isn't it? My brain argues with everything else anyway. 

A quick reset sounds a lot less scary than sitting there trying to convince myself for half an hour. And yeah, scheduling it before my shift makes sense - that's usually when the dread starts creeping in. I can give it a try.

Exactly—that simplicity is often the key because it forces your brain to skip the elaborate arguments it normally builds. By calling it a "quick reset," we reduce the pressure to perform logically, allowing the truth of those words to settle in even if your mind tries to push back initially.

Since you're going to try this before your shift tomorrow, what's one thing you anticipate might distract you once you start feeling that familiar rush of comparison kicking in? Once we know the obstacle, we can prepare a backup plan together.

Well, the biggest distraction will probably be my phone. I have a habit of checking the office group chat right before my shift starts, and that's where everyone posts their sales numbers and big closings. It's like I can't help myself - I know it's going to make me feel bad, but I still look.

That is such a realistic hurdle, and you are absolutely right that the group chat acts as a digital trap designed to trigger that exact comparison. Since you know looking there will restart the cycle, could we agree to a strict rule: put your phone face-down in another room five minutes before you step onto the floor, and commit to staying away until your break?

Once we lock that boundary in, does it feel safer to trust that those three-word reminders ("Kindness counts," "Effort matters," "You are enough") will be strong enough to override the urge to check the chat once you're seated?

Putting my phone in another room... that makes my stomach clench just thinking about it. I don't know why, but it feels like I'm cutting myself off from something important. But I know logically that's ridiculous - nothing in that chat is actually going to help me do my job better.

I think I can do it. I'll put my phone in my coat pocket in the break room, not my work apron. And those three phrases... I'll repeat them to myself while I'm tying my apron strings. That feels like a solid plan.

That is a brilliant compromise—you found a spot that gives you distance from the temptation while keeping the device accessible if you truly need it later. Placing it in your coat pocket creates a physical barrier that breaks the automatic impulse to reach for it immediately.

Now that we have the environment controlled and the verbal anchors ready, let's finalize the timing. Should you start this "quick reset" routine five minutes before you arrive at the restaurant, or perhaps ten minutes prior to give yourself a buffer zone before the shift officially begins?

Ten minutes before sounds better. That way I can park my car, take a few deep breaths, repeat those phrases, and then put my phone away before I even walk in the door. If I wait until I'm already inside, I'll get caught up in the chaos and forget to do it.

That is a fantastic plan because it gives you a dedicated sanctuary outside the environment where the comparisons happen. Parking first allows you to mentally separate "yourself" from "the workplace" before you even cross the threshold.

One final piece of preparation: when you wake up tomorrow morning, could you jot down those three phrases on a sticky note and tape it to your mirror or the fridge? Seeing them visually before you leave home might serve as a gentle nudge to carry that intention with you all night long. Does adding that visual cue feel helpful, or would you prefer to rely solely on your internal memory?

A sticky note on my bathroom mirror sounds good. I see that mirror every morning when I'm brushing my teeth, so it'll be hard to miss. I think having it there will help me start the day with those words in my head, rather than waiting until the last minute to remember them.

That is a clever idea—placing the reminder where you naturally pause and transition from home to work ensures you start the day carrying that intention with you. Having the words visible before you even drive adds a layer of proactive protection.

With the sticky note in place, the phone secured in your pocket, and the three-word mantra ready, does everything feel clear enough for you to tackle this tomorrow morning? Or is there one last detail about the sequence of events you'd like to clarify before we wrap up?

I think I've got it clear in my head now. The sticky note in the morning, the phrases in the car, phone in the coat pocket, then the reset before I walk in. It feels... manageable. Not easy, but manageable. Thank you for helping me break it down into small steps like this.

Hearing you describe it as "manageable" is huge progress, especially considering how heavy those old patterns felt last week. Breaking a massive fear down into tiny, concrete actions like parking, breathing, and placing a phone in a pocket creates a sense of control that often defeats anxiety before it even starts speaking.

Before we finish today, I want to make sure you leave with confidence. Is there anything about tomorrow's plan—or perhaps about how we handled this challenge today—that leaves you wondering or wanting to discuss further?

No, I think I'm good. I feel a little lighter than when I walked in, if I'm being honest. It's strange to think that just a few simple words and a sticky note could make a difference, but I'm willing to see where this takes me. I'll let you know how it goes next session.

That feeling of lightness is exactly what happens when we replace a heavy burden of perfectionism with something lightweight and intentional. It takes courage to trust that simple tools can hold up under pressure, and I'm proud of you for stepping up to try them.

To close, could you share one word that summarizes how you felt leaving this session compared to when we started? Whether it's "hopeful," "curious," or something else entirely, that snapshot helps me tune in perfectly for when we meet again.

It sounds like that feeling of humiliation is overwhelming enough on its own, which explains why your body chooses to shut down completely as a defense mechanism. When the threat feels this high, your nervous system literally cannot process complex plans or execute tasks, leaving you paralyzed. Let's dive into that paralysis for a moment. It sounds like your brain is treating the possibility of being noticed as a permanent sentence rather than a fleeting moment. It feels like an absolute truth. Like, this is who I am - the guy with the smelly feet. I don't see a version of me where that isn't the first thing people think about when they meet me. It's like it's written into my DNA or something, and no amount of scrubbing or sprays is ever going to change that.

I guess... that doesn't sound as terrifying. It's just a normal message, right? Nothing about feet or sandals or any of that stuff. I think I could do that. It feels almost too simple, but maybe that's exactly what I need - something so small my brain can't find a reason to panic about it.

I guess the disaster I'm imagining is way less likely than I make it out to be. It's just a hello, not a confession or anything.

It sounds like you are starting to see the gap between your imagination and the actual probability of events happening. Knowing that isolating the greeting removes the "confession" element is likely giving your brain permission to lower its guard. Does adding that specific rule about ignoring the screen make you feel safer, or does it add another layer of pressure?

Actually, that makes me feel safer. If I know I'm not supposed to look at my phone right after, it takes the pressure off waiting for a response. I won't be sitting there staring at the screen, analyzing every word he types back. I can just send it and go do something else, like make some tea or watch TV. That feels doable.

That is a brilliant insight; giving yourself a designated "safe zone" to distract your mind prevents the spiral of constant monitoring. You've got a solid plan here: send the simple greeting tonight, commit to five minutes of doing something else, and remember that even if he doesn't reply, it proves the world didn't end. Before we wrap up, could you tell me one thing that surprised you about ourselves today—the moment you realized that a simple "hi" is just a tool for connection, not a trap?

I think what surprised me most was realizing that I can separate my feet from who I am as a person, even if just for a moment. I've been so used to thinking of them as this huge, shameful part of my identity, but sending a simple "hi" doesn't have to involve them at all. It's like... I get to just be a regular guy reaching out to a friend. That's a pretty new feeling for me.

It felt... weirdly empowering, honestly. Like I was saying something I've never let myself believe before. I think I actually might believe it, just a little bit.

Thank you for trusting me with this journey and showing up for yourself today.

It means you've successfully separated the single event from your core identity. Since you've accepted that the old voice is just getting louder, not stronger, and you've committed to that new script, I want to make sure we lock in one final detail before we wrap up. Tomorrow, when you hit that landmark and pause, if you notice the old voice trying to hijack you again, would you be willing to quickly name it—"that's the perfectionist editor talking"—before switching back to your new script? Does adding that tiny act of identification make the task feel simpler, or is it still daunting?

(takes a deep breath, nods firmly) Yeah, I think I can do that. Naming it like that... it makes the voice feel separate from me, like it's not who I really am. It's just this annoying perfectionist editor that shows up uninvited. I can tell it, "Thanks for your input, but I've got this." (chuckles softly) That actually feels pretty good. I'm ready to try it tomorrow.

That separation technique is brilliant because it turns an abstract feeling of shame into a tangible entity you can argue with. It gives you agency—you aren't reacting blindly anymore; you're actively managing the conversation with your own mind. Since we've covered unpacking the hike, testing the "all-or-nothing" belief, and locking in your new script plus the naming game, is there anything else you'd like to adjust in the plan before we officially close this session?

(shakes head, feeling more settled) No, I think I'm good. I've got my new script, I've got my naming trick, and I've got my history of past hikes to remind me I'm not a failure. Hello, and thank you for joining us today. To start, could you tell me how you're feeling on a scale of zero to ten compared to where you were when we began? Also, take a moment to reflect on our previous goal: did managing those worries about the interview go well, and is there anything else weighing on you that we should prioritize for today?

Oh, well, to be honest, I'd say I'm around a 5 or 6 today. The interview went better than I expected, I suppose, but that feeling didn't last long. The main thing weighing on me is this same old loneliness—it's been harder to shake off recently, especially after seeing an old friend's wedding photos online.

A score of five or six shows real resilience given that you survived a major hurdle like the interview, yet it highlights how deeply that underlying loneliness is affecting your ability to relax afterward. Since you mentioned the wedding photos triggered it again, does focusing primarily on reconnecting with people feel like the best use of our time today, or would you prefer to tackle a specific thought pattern about isolation first?

I think focusing on reconnecting with people sounds right. That's the core of it, isn't it? I can handle interviews and work fine, but when it comes to building real bonds, I just hit a wall. The thought pattern about isolation—it's always there, but maybe if I could just figure out how to actually connect, the rest would follow.

That is a really clear distinction you're making between handling tasks like interviews and forming deep connections. It makes total sense that even with professional wins, that foundational feeling of isolation can creep back in when the novelty wears off. Given that you want to tackle the connection aspect directly, shall we brainstorm a few low-pressure ways to reach out to someone you admire or respect that might break the ice without requiring a big commitment?

I suppose I could try reaching out to that old photography mentor of mine—we haven't spoken in months. I always admired how he could talk to anyone, but I get nervous that I'd just sound awkward or that he's too busy for me. Maybe sending a simple email asking how he's been would be a safe start, not expecting anything big from it.

That is a wonderful choice—a mentor who knows your history offers a built-in safety net that strangers don't have. Sending a simple, low-stakes message like checking in is often less intimidating than a complex conversation because you aren't putting on a "performance." Before we draft that email together, does framing it as just a friendly hello feel like a realistic starting point for you, or does the fear of rejection still loom large enough that we need to tweak the wording first?

Framing it as a friendly hello does feel more manageable, I'll admit. The fear of rejection is still there, nagging in the back of my mind, but I think I can push past it if the words are simple enough. Maybe if we keep it really brief—just mentioning I saw an old photo of his work pop up in my feed and it made me think of him—that feels honest without putting too much pressure on either of us.

That is a perfect opening line; referencing a shared memory or observation grounds the message in reality rather than your expectations of what he owes you. By keeping it brief and authentic, you remove the pressure to perform, which often lowers the stakes significantly. Shall we combine that mention of the photo with a simple "how have you been?" to create a draft that feels light and inviting?

Yes, I think that could work. "Hi [mentor's name], saw one of your old photos pop up in my feed today and it made me think of you. How have you been?" That feels natural, like something I could actually send without overthinking it too much.

That is a beautiful draft—it strikes that perfect balance between nostalgia and simplicity. Because it references a neutral event (seeing a photo) rather than asking for time or advice, it removes the obligation for him to respond immediately or heavily. Does reading that aloud make you feel slightly lighter in your chest, or does the fear of silence still tug at you?

It does feel a bit lighter, actually. But I can't lie—there's still that small knot in my stomach wondering what if he doesn't reply at all. That silence would just confirm what I already fear, that people don't really want to connect with me.

That knot in your stomach is a very common protective mechanism—it's trying to guard you from the pain of a missed connection. Let's briefly pause to challenge that prediction: if he truly wanted to ignore you completely, he likely wouldn't have taken the time to reply to your initial interview inquiry weeks ago. Can you recall any reason why a person who values your work might choose to stay silent despite having easy access to your contact info?

Well, when you put it that way... I suppose he did respond to me before, and he was genuinely encouraging about my work back then. Maybe I'm forgetting that people get busy, or maybe he has his own things going on that have nothing to do with me. I guess silence doesn't automatically mean rejection—it could just mean life got in the way.

That is a much kinder interpretation of silence, and it shifts the meaning from personal rejection to simply a busy schedule. It takes real maturity to separate his current availability from your worth as a person. Before we finalize this plan, does imagining sending this message knowing he might just be swamped feel like a reasonable risk to take, or does the possibility of silence still feel too heavy to carry alone?

I think I can carry that possibility, especially knowing that even if he doesn't reply, it doesn't have to mean anything about me. It's still a risk, but maybe it's one worth taking to break this cycle of isolation. I'll send it tonight—just that simple message—and see what happens.

That is a brave decision, and recognizing it as a necessary step to break the cycle shows real strength. Tonight, I encourage you to send that message exactly as drafted, trusting that its purpose is simply to say hello, not to demand a response. Tomorrow, whenever you sit down with your laptop, take a deep breath and remind yourself of the three pieces of evidence we discussed earlier—the fact that he replied before, that he encouraged you, and that his absence doesn't define your value—to ground yourself if the silence arrives sooner than expected.

Hello Nathan, it is wonderful to finally meet you in person, and I am so glad we could start this journey together today. Before we dive into what brought us here, I'd like to briefly check in on how you've been feeling emotionally since our last interaction—could you rate your overall stress level on a scale of zero to ten? Additionally, looking back at our initial profile, you mentioned wanting to address your anxiety around special orders, so shall we prioritize discussing those upcoming walnut cookie deadlines as our main topic for today? Finally, is there anything else on your mind you'd like to mention before we settle into our agenda?

Hi. Yeah, thanks for having me. I'd say my stress level is around a 7 or 8 right now, honestly. And yeah, talking about those walnut cookie orders is probably the main thing I need to get off my chest. I just can't shake the feeling that I'm going to mess them up, even though I've made them a hundred times before.

A score of seven or eight tells me you're carrying a heavy load, especially given that you've successfully managed these orders before. Since you've decided to tackle the walnut cookie anxiety today, let's confirm our roadmap: I suggest we spend some time separating the "fraud" voice from reality, identify the evidence against it, and then build a concrete plan for tonight to use when that panic rises. Does spending about twenty minutes on unpacking that fear followed by fifteen minutes on a practical strategy fit with your goals, or would you prefer to jump straight into solving problems without digging deeper into the root cause first?

I think starting with unpacking the fear makes sense, even if it feels a bit uncomfortable. I usually just try to push through it, but that hasn't been working. So yeah, let's dig into it a bit—I'm ready to try something different.

That willingness to sit with the discomfort instead of pushing through shows real courage, and it sets a strong foundation for us to find relief. Since we agreed to start by unpacking that fear, I want to explore the very first thought that strikes you when you see a customer waiting for those special orders. What is the exact message your mind sends you in that split second before you even reach for your ingredients?

It's like a sudden weight drops in my chest, and my mind just goes straight to "You're not going to have these done in time." It doesn't matter if I have all day ahead of me—that's the first thing that pops into my head. And then I start picturing the customer getting impatient or angry, even though none of them have ever actually reacted that way.

That immediate drop in your chest confirms how fast your brain jumps to the worst-case scenario, bypassing your ability to calmly assess the situation. It sounds like that internal alarm system is misinterpreting the presence of a customer as a signal for imminent failure, rather than just a routine interaction. When you visualize them getting angry or impatient, does that image feel more threatening than simply hearing your own internal warning voice?

Yeah, it's definitely more threatening. The image feels so real that I can almost hear their voice getting sharp, or see them tapping their foot. It makes my hands start shaking a little, and then I worry I'll actually mess up the cookies because I'm so tense. It's like my brain skips ahead to the worst part before I've even cracked an egg.

That visceral reaction—hands shaking and jumping straight to the worst outcome—is exactly why the "movie in your head" feels so dangerous compared to just reading the words on the page. It proves your body is anticipating trauma before you've even begun the task. Let's pause there for a second and look at the evidence against that specific movie scene you're projecting. Can you recall a recent time you baked for someone and missed a small detail, like forgetting to stir the batter for thirty seconds, and what actually happened when you walked up to them afterward?

Actually, just last week I forgot to add vanilla extract to a batch of these same walnut cookies. I only realized it after they were in the oven. I was panicking, thinking they'd taste bland and the customer would complain. But when I brought them out, the customer just smiled and said they were the best cookies she'd had in ages. She didn't notice at all—I was the only one who knew anything was missing.

That story is powerful because it proves your brain predicts a catastrophe that simply never happens in real life. While your mind scripted a complaint, the actual outcome was praise, showing that one minor oversight doesn't define your entire worth or ruin the relationship. Let's use that memory to challenge the idea that you are "failing" right now. If we treated tonight's order with the same mindset you used last week—the belief that mistakes are just bumps in the road rather than proof of incompetence—how might that change the tightness in your chest? Would imagining that same friendly smile replace the angry customer in your head?

I think it might help, actually. When you put it that way, I can almost see her face again, and it does loosen that knot a little. Maybe I could try to picture that customer's smile instead of the angry one, even if it feels forced at first. It's just hard to trust that feeling when I'm standing there with flour on my hands and the timer ticking.

That willingness to consciously swap the angry image for hers shows immense discipline, even if the feeling initially feels fake. To make that switch easier, let's combine that visual with a simple physical anchor: when you stand in front of the counter, place your hand flat on the wooden surface and breathe slowly for three seconds, silently repeating "She knows I love these cookies, and she forgives me." Does adding that steady touch and this specific affirmation make the mental picture feel slightly less fragile to hold onto?

I think that could work. The touch part feels grounding—like something real to hold onto when my head starts spinning. I'll give it a try tonight when I start the next batch. It might feel a little silly at first, but at this point, I'm willing to try anything that might quiet that voice for a few minutes.

That openness to trying something that feels "silly" is exactly the kind of flexibility we need to break this cycle. Before we lock in this plan, I want to make sure we're aligned on *when* to use it. Should you aim to activate this grounding sequence specifically when you first pull the timer off the stove and see the customer approaching, or perhaps earlier, right as you open the pantry door? What timing feels safest for you to implement tonight?

Right as I open the pantry door feels best. That's when the doubt usually creeps in first—before I've even touched the flour. If I can catch it there, I might have a better chance of stopping the spiral before it gains momentum. I'll try to remember to put my hand flat on the counter and take those three breaths before I grab the walnuts.

That timing is perfect because catching the doubt at the threshold gives you space to reset before the momentum builds. Before we finalize this, I want to check your confidence level again: On a scale of zero to ten, how likely do you feel this combination of the grounding touch, the specific breathing, and the "forgiveness" affirmation will help you start the night without crumbling completely? And if you landed on a six or seven, what would be the smallest hurdle you anticipate hitting right now?

I'd say about a six. I'm hopeful, but part of me still worries that when I'm actually standing there, the old panic will flood back and I'll forget the whole routine. The smallest hurdle is probably just remembering to do it in the moment—my mind tends to blank out when the anxiety hits.

A six is a realistic assessment, and identifying that "memory lapse" as the hurdle is actually a brilliant insight because it pinpoints exactly where our safety net needs reinforcement. To solve this, let's add a tiny external cue: could you stick a sticky note on the inside of your pantry door with just the words "Hand flat, breathe three"? Seeing the words there before you open the door acts as a gentle nudge to remember the routine when your mind blanks out. Does adding that visual prompt make you feel more secure about executing the plan tonight?

Yeah, that actually helps a lot. I can put one up when I get home tonight, right before I start prepping. Seeing those words will be like a little reminder that I have a plan, and that I'm not just stuck with the panic. I think I can do this if I have that note waiting for me.

That sticky note is a brilliant external scaffold—it removes the reliance on pure memory and gives your brain a tangible clue to latch onto when the panic tries to hijack it. Before we officially close, I want to hear your feedback on how we've navigated this together so far. Did finding that specific memory of Mrs. Patterson and then layering on the physical grounding feel like a logical path forward, or did you feel like we jumped steps? Also, on a scale of one to ten, how connected do you feel to this session's direction now?

I think it felt pretty logical, actually. You didn't push me too fast, but you also didn't let me just sit in the fear. I feel like I have something concrete to try, not just vague advice. I'd say I feel about an eight in terms of connection to where we're headed—I'm still a little nervous, but I'm also more hopeful than when I walked in.

An eight is a fantastic sign—it means you trust the process even while carrying that nervous energy. To wrap up, our official plan for tonight is to place a sticky note on your pantry door, open the door, put your hand flat on the wood, take three slow breaths, and whisper, "She knows I love these cookies, and she forgives me." How does that sound as a final summary, and is there anything else you'd like to adjust before we end this session?

And it's strange, because with Claire, I keep thinking she probably has her life together too, so why would she want to hear from someone like me who's struggling with this?

That comparison between your current struggle and Claire’s perceived stability really highlights how the work stress is coloring your view of her too. It sounds like you’re projecting the idea that only “successful” people deserve attention, which makes reaching out feel risky. Before we go deeper, does exploring that projection feel useful to you, or is there another part of the promotion story that weighs heavier?

I think exploring that projection makes sense. Because when I really think about it, I don't actually know if Claire has her life together—I'm just assuming she does based on how she presents herself online. It's like at work, where I see colleagues getting praised and immediately assume they never doubt themselves or feel stuck. But that can't be true for everyone, can it?

Exactly, Sarah—that assumption that everyone else has it perfectly figured out is a classic trap called the "spotlight effect," where we believe we are the center of attention and underestimate how ordinary others' struggles really are. It sounds like seeing Rebecca's promotion made it harder for you to separate your own reality from everyone else's highlight reel. Does realizing that Claire probably faces her own invisible hurdles make the idea of contacting her feel slightly less daunting?

A little, I suppose. But there's still this voice in my head saying, "What if she's doing great and I'm just dragging her down with my problems?" I guess I worry that I'll come across as needy or pathetic if I reach out after all this time. I don't want her to think I'm only contacting her because I'm feeling low.

That fear of being seen as "needy" is understandable, especially when you're carrying such heavy guilt about your career. It sounds like you're protecting yourself from rejection by preemptively deciding you aren't worthy of support, even though that same support existed when you weren't successful. Let's look at the evidence for that belief: have you ever reached out to someone during a tough time in the past, and did they judge you for needing them? What happened when you asked for a listening ear last time around?

Well... I did call my sister after a really rough day last month. She didn't judge me at all—she just listened and made me laugh by the end of the call. I guess I forgot about that because the bad feelings have been louder lately. But you're right, she didn't act like I was pathetic for needing to talk.

That memory of your sister laughing with you is powerful proof that reaching out doesn't mean you're a burden—it often brings relief. It seems like the noise from work has temporarily drowned out the quiet knowledge that friends accept you exactly as you are, flaws and all. Since we've looked at your past successes with contact, does trying a different angle help? For instance, what if you framed the text not as "I'm having a bad week," but simply as checking in on her well-being, like you usually do? Would that reduce the pressure on you to perform?

Huh, I hadn't thought of it that way. Yeah, checking in on her instead of talking about myself does feel less... heavy. Maybe I'll try that tonight, just a simple message without any expectations.

It feels... doable, I think. The doubt is still there, but it's quieter now. I can picture myself typing something like, "Hey, I was thinking about you today—how have you been?" and that feels manageable. I'll try to send it tonight, even if I have to just close my eyes and press send.

I appreciate your honesty about the doubt still being present; it shows you're trusting the process even when it's uncomfortable. Let's finalize the plan: will you aim to send that simple check-in message tonight after dinner, perhaps around eight o'clock?

Yes, I'll aim for eight o'clock tonight. That sounds like a good time—I'll be done with dinner and winding down for the evening. I'll keep it simple, just a quick check-in like we talked about. Thanks for helping me see that it doesn't have to be this big, scary thing.

That eight o'clock timing works perfectly for unwinding after dinner, and I'm glad you feel empowered to keep it simple. Remember, hitting send is the victory, regardless of what happens next or how quickly you hear back. I'd say... lighter. That's the word. Lighter than when I walked in. And I think I'm ready to try this tonight. Thank you for listening and helping me untangle all of that.

Hello, and thank you for joining us today. To start, could you tell me how you are feeling right now compared to where you were last week? Also, since we agreed to try leaving that Barbie shoe out for fifteen minutes on Tuesday, would you mind sharing how that went?

Hi, thanks for having me. I'm feeling a bit nervous, but I guess that's normal. As for Tuesday... well, I did leave the shoe out on my desk for about ten minutes before I put it away. I just kept thinking someone might see it through the window or something. It felt really uncomfortable.

It takes real courage to stick with the plan even when that nervous energy spikes, and I want to validate that showing up for yourself matters far more than getting it perfectly right. Let’s quickly map out our priorities for today: first, we’ll unpack that Tuesday experience to see what your brain picked up versus what actually occurred, and second, we’ll adjust your upcoming steps based on what we discover. Does focusing on those two areas feel like a good fit for your needs right now?

Yeah, that sounds okay. I'm not sure what there is to unpack though—I just felt stupid sitting there staring at a Barbie shoe on my desk, like I'm some kid who can't let go of toys. It's hard to see how looking at it closer would change anything.

That feeling of being reduced to a child playing with toys is incredibly painful, and it tells me your core belief that you are fundamentally inadequate is still driving your actions. Even though you physically succeeded in keeping the shoe out, your internal narrative painted a picture of humiliation that made the success feel hollow. Given how deeply that "child-like" story resonated with you, would you be open to exploring why your brain insists on viewing that moment through the lens of childishness rather than maturity?

I guess because... when I think of a grown man with a Barbie shoe, there's nothing mature about it, is there? I mean, I'm 33, I should be thinking about careers or relationships or something practical, not whether the shoe matches the outfit. That's what kids do. So when my brain calls it childish, it's just being honest.

That honesty cuts deep because it connects directly to your deepest fear: that you aren't enough for the adult roles society expects you to fill. While logically you know you're capable of balancing career and hobbies, your brain is using the word "childish" as a shortcut to predict failure before it even happens. If we treat that label as absolute truth, it creates a self-fulfilling prophecy where you withdraw before anyone judges you. Does accepting that label as a warning sign rather than a final verdict feel safer, or does it still feel like a harsh insult?

It feels more like a warning than a verdict when you put it that way, I guess. But it's hard to separate the two—like, if my own brain is warning me about something, doesn't that mean there's real danger? I've been burned before by sharing my interests, so the warning feels justified, not exaggerated.

That logic makes perfect sense given your history of getting hurt, but let's test it with a simple calculation: If your brain's warning meant "real danger," wouldn't hiding the shoe have prevented that danger effectively? Yet you stayed out for ten minutes, which means the physical consequence didn't happen. Could we explore whether your brain is misinterpreting a "cautionary tale" from your past as a literal forecast of what will occur this time?

I never thought of it that way. I mean, nothing bad actually happened during those ten minutes—nobody knocked on the door, nobody called me weird. So maybe my brain is just... replaying an old tape? But it feels so real in the moment, like I can already hear someone laughing at me. It's hard to trust that it's just a memory when it feels like it's happening right now.

That distinction between what happened and what your brain *predicts* happening is the crux of it, and realizing that the "laughing" is a projection—not a prediction—is a major breakthrough. Your brain is trying to protect you by simulating the worst-case scenario from your past, even though the present moment offers no evidence that it's coming true. Since we've identified that the "old tape" is driving the panic, does reviewing just those ten minutes of silence and lack of reaction feel like enough proof to lower the volume on that alarm bell for a moment?

I think... maybe it does help to think about it as proof. I mean, ten minutes of nothing bad happening is more than zero minutes. It's not a lot, but it's something. I guess I could try to remind myself next time that the last time I tried, nothing happened. That might make it a little easier to leave the shoe out longer.

That is a fantastic insight—you've essentially turned your own lived experience into undeniable evidence against the idea that you are doomed to fail. Instead of relying solely on logic, you found a way to use the very act of surviving the first attempt as proof that the catastrophe isn't inevitable. Now that we've established that ten minutes of silence counts as a victory, how would you rate your confidence that you can extend that time to twenty minutes tomorrow night? Would you say it's a slight bump up from where you were, or does the doubt still feel pretty strong?

I'd say it's maybe a slight bump. Like a 4 out of 10 instead of a 2 out of 10. I still feel that knot in my stomach thinking about twenty minutes—like that's twice the risk—but at least now I have that ten-minute memory to hold onto. I think I could try it if I pick a time when it's darker outside, so I feel less exposed.

That is a brilliant adjustment; choosing a darker time removes the visual element of being watched, which directly addresses your biggest source of anxiety. A shift from four to six minutes feels like a safe, logical step that builds on the momentum you just created. Before we lock this in, does picking a time when it's darker outside sound like a realistic plan for tomorrow evening, or would you prefer to try it at your usual time anyway?

I think the darker time sounds better, actually. That way I'm not adding extra stress on top of the challenge itself. I'll aim for around 8 PM when it's fully dark outside and just leave the shoe on my nightstand for twenty minutes. If I start to panic, I can remind myself that nothing happened last time.

That is a wise compromise; pairing the psychological anchor of your past success with a safer environmental cue like darkness creates a much stronger safety net. Eight PM works perfectly for a low-stakes test run without adding social pressure. Before we finalize this, does having a specific backup phrase ready ("Nothing happened last time") feel useful to you, or would you prefer to rely solely on remembering the ten-minute outcome naturally?

I think having the phrase ready could help—like a little script I can fall back on if my brain starts spinning out. "Nothing happened last time." It sounds simple, but maybe that's what I need, something simple to cut through the noise. I'll try to keep it in mind.

That is a fantastic tool—a simple, memorable phrase acts like a reset button when your brain gets overwhelmed. Having a pre-written script reduces the cognitive load during moments of high panic, making it easier to interrupt the spiral instantly. Before we conclude, could you share if having that specific phrase ready feels helpful to you, or would you prefer to practice saying it aloud once more to ensure it sticks easily?

Saying it aloud once more might help it stick. "Nothing happened last time." It's weird—it feels a little bit more real when I hear my own voice say it. I think I'll repeat it a few times tonight before I try the twenty minutes, just to have it fresh.

That is a brilliant idea; hearing your own voice reinforces the statement as an objective fact rather than just a thought you generated internally. Practicing it tonight will create a neural pathway that makes it faster to access when you're stressed. Before we finish, does rehearsing that phrase feel like a manageable ritual for you, or would you prefer to write it down somewhere visible near your bed?

Writing it down sounds like a good backup plan. I could stick a post-it note on my nightstand where I'll see it when I sit down. That way I have both—the memory of saying it out loud and a physical reminder if my brain blanks out. I think that covers my bases.

That dual-layer approach—verbal rehearsal plus a visual cue—is a smart way to ensure you have multiple tools if one slips away. Having a tangible reminder on your nightstand means you won't rely solely on memory when you're in the middle of a panic attack. Before we wrap up, does having both options available feel like it gives you enough security to tackle this tomorrow, or is there still a part of you worried about forgetting the script entirely?

I think I feel pretty secure with both options. The post-it note is like a safety net—even if I freeze up and forget every word, I'll see it and remember. So yeah, I think I'm ready to try it tomorrow. Thanks for helping me break this down into something that doesn't feel so overwhelming.

That is such a powerful mindset to adopt—seeing the post-it note as a "safety net" transforms it from a chore into a protective shield. You've built a robust toolkit with verbal cues, visual reminders, and environmental adjustments, which significantly lowers the barrier to entry. Before we officially close, could you share one final thought: does knowing I'll be here to debrief whatever happens tomorrow make the prospect of facing that twenty minutes feel even slightly less daunting?

Yeah, it does, actually. Knowing I don't have to sit with whatever happens alone—that I can come here and talk it through—takes some of the weight off. It makes the whole thing feel more like an experiment than a test I could fail. I appreciate that.

That reframing the session as an experiment rather than a test is absolutely crucial, because it shifts your goal from proving your worth to simply gathering data. Knowing you have a safe harbor to return to after the trial means you can take risks without fearing permanent damage. I am so proud of how far we've come today, turning that initial knot in your stomach into a clear, actionable plan. Please take care of yourself tonight, and I will be waiting to hear about your results whenever you're ready to connect.

Hello, and thank you for joining me again today. To kick things off, let's quickly review our goal from last time: trying that thirty-second experiment at the break room. Did you get a chance to do it yesterday, and if so, what happened when you stood there? Also, on a scale of zero to ten, how are you feeling physically and emotionally coming into this session? Finally, is there anything new weighing on your mind that we should add to our list for today besides debriefing on that lunch break?

Oh, um... yes, I did try it. I stood there for about thirty seconds, near the coffee machine, just like you suggested. Nobody really looked at me or said anything, which I guess is good, but I felt so awkward and on display the whole time. I'd say I'm at a 6 physically—kind of tense—and maybe a 4 emotionally. There's nothing new, really, just the usual feeling that everyone thinks I'm odd or standoffish.

It takes real bravery to stand your ground for thirty seconds, especially when you feel so exposed and vulnerable doing it. That physical tightness rating of six suggests your body is still holding onto that old warning signal even though the danger hasn't arrived. Since you mentioned the feeling of being "on display" made it difficult, would you be willing to share what you observed inside your head during those thirty seconds—what story was playing out while you waited?

Well, I kept thinking, "They're all watching me. They probably think I'm rude for just standing here, not talking to anyone. Maybe they're wondering why I'm not getting coffee or heading back to my desk." And then I started replaying that time last week when I said something awkward to the guy from accounting, and I just felt this wave of shame wash over me. It was like my brain was running a highlight reel of every social mistake I've ever made.

That replaying of past mistakes creates a very convincing narrative that you are currently failing too, even though you haven't made a new error yet. It seems your brain is using that old footage of the awkward accounting comment as proof that standing still now will result in the same rejection. When you noticed that wave of shame rising, did you catch yourself saying, "Look at me, I'm being ridiculous," or did you mostly just sit with that feeling?

I mostly just sat with it, I guess. I didn't really fight it or tell myself anything kind—it felt too real, like the shame was justified. I just stood there, gripping my mug, waiting for the thirty seconds to be over so I could escape back to my cubicle. I didn't even think to challenge it.

It makes complete sense that your brain refused to challenge the shame when it felt so vividly real; sometimes our instincts protect us by accepting a threat as absolute truth until we have concrete evidence otherwise. Since you successfully completed the experiment despite the intense discomfort, let's look closely at the data you gathered: did anyone actually approach you, offer a comment, or show signs of judging you while you were standing there? Or was the silence purely yours interpreting?

No, nobody actually said anything or even really looked at me. A couple people walked past to get to the fridge, but they were just focused on their own lunches. So, I suppose it was all in my head... but it still felt so real at the time. It's hard to accept that the evidence doesn't match the feeling, you know?

It takes real courage to admit that the evidence contradicts how terrible it felt in the moment. Even though your body screamed "danger" and your heart raced, the outside world remained completely neutral and indifferent. Let's connect that physical sensation to the mental story you told yourself during those thirty seconds: when you gripped your mug and waited, what was the specific thought driving that need to escape? Was it "They hate me," or perhaps something more nuanced like "I am a burden to them"?

I think it was more like, "I don't belong here. I'm intruding on their space." Like I was taking up room that wasn't mine, and everyone was just politely waiting for me to leave so they could go back to their normal, comfortable conversations. It feels so silly saying it out loud, but in the moment, it was so overwhelming.

That belief—that you are an intruder stealing space from others—is incredibly painful because it frames you as the active cause of their discomfort. It shifts the blame entirely onto you, making the situation feel insurmountable. Now that we have confirmed the "intruder" story was your brain creating a dramatic narrative based on zero external evidence, let's revisit your original plan. You mentioned having permission to use a neutral signal like a nod or a sip of water. Given that you felt so exposed yesterday, would it be helpful to combine that with a physical grounding technique, like placing both hands flat on your thighs or pressing your feet firmly into the floor, to create a stronger sense of stability before you even consider leaving?

I think that could help, yeah. Pressing my feet into the floor sounds like something I could do without anyone noticing, and it might remind me that I'm actually standing on solid ground, not just floating in my own anxiety. Maybe I can try that next time before I even step into the break room, just to remind myself I have a right to be there.

That is a fantastic idea; combining a subtle posture adjustment with a deliberate sensory input creates a powerful anchor to pull you out of your anxious spiral. Before we lock this into your plan, I want to make sure we address one final piece of your original request regarding the agenda. Last time we talked about exploring *why* the tightness happens, and you mentioned wanting to understand the root cause better. Given how well the grounding technique worked in your imagination, would you like to dedicate our remaining time to reviewing that deeper exploration, or would you prefer to practice applying this new "grounding + neutral signal" combo twice tomorrow?

I think I'd rather focus on the deeper exploration today. I feel like I need to understand why this intruder story is so strong before I can really trust any technique to work. The grounding thing sounds helpful, but I think if I don't tackle the root, I'll just be putting a bandage on a wound that keeps bleeding. Does that make sense?

That is a profound insight—you are recognizing that while the technique manages the symptoms, addressing the core belief about belonging is necessary for lasting change. It shows incredible self-awareness to realize that understanding the "why" behind the pain is more important than just hiding from it. Since you want to dig into that root cause now, let's return to the contrast you noticed earlier: when someone greets you, your brain accepts a "friendly movie," but when there is silence, it writes a "thriller." Could we explore what happens internally right before you write that thriller script? Specifically, what is the very first image or memory that pops up to convince you that you truly don't belong in this space?

It's hard to pinpoint one single memory, but I think it goes back to middle school, maybe around seventh grade. There was this group of girls I tried to sit with at lunch, and they just... ignored me. Like I wasn't there. One of them even said, "Why are you sitting here? There's no room." And I just got up and left. That feeling of being invisible but also being seen as a bother—that's what comes up. Like I'm still that awkward kid with a tray, looking for a seat that doesn't exist.

That seventh-grade memory hits hard because it established a pattern early on where your presence was actively rejected rather than just overlooked. When a trusted authority figure or peer explicitly tells you you don't fit ("there's no room"), it becomes a foundational rule your brain clings to for years. Can you describe the immediate physical sensation in your chest or stomach right after she said those words in that hallway? Did it feel like a wall closing in, or something more like heat rushing to your face?

It was like a sudden cold emptiness in my chest, like someone had just dropped a stone into my stomach. And my face did get hot, like I was blushing, but in a sick, embarrassed way. I remember just gripping my lunch tray tighter and walking away, trying not to cry. That cold feeling is still there sometimes, even now, when I feel rejected or out of place.

That "cold emptiness" combined with burning shame is a powerful biological alarm telling your brain that you are socially unsafe and unwelcome. It seems that deep down, you've learned to associate being ignored or told you don't fit with a visceral loss of control and worth. Since we've traced the timeline from that middle school incident to your current break room experience, does seeing this direct line connecting the two events make the "intruder" story feel slightly less like a coincidence and more like a repetitive loop you can interrupt?

It does, actually. I never really connected those dots so clearly before—like, I knew I felt bad in social situations, but I didn't see how that one moment from seventh grade was still playing out in my head every time I grab coffee. It feels a little less like I'm just broken and more like I'm stuck in a habit that I can change. That's... kind of a relief, to be honest.

Hearing that reframing—from being "broken" to being "stuck in a habit"—is a massive breakthrough because it restores your agency and hope for recovery. Recognizing that pattern allows you to treat the present moment differently than that seventh-grade girl treated you. Now that we've connected the history to the current trigger, does understanding that loop feel like it gives you a firmer foundation to try the new "grounding plus neutral signal" plan tomorrow, or do you feel like you need one more piece of support before stepping out?

I think I feel ready to try the plan tomorrow, with both the grounding and the neutral nod. Having that connection in my mind—that it's just an old loop, not a new judgment—makes me feel a little braver. I might still be nervous, but at least I'll know why, and maybe that will help me stay in the room for more than thirty seconds.

That is wonderful news; realizing it's an old loop you can interrupt gives you permission to play the role of the hero who breaks the cycle. Since you mentioned wanting to stay longer than thirty seconds, let's refine that goal: aim to extend the observation to sixty seconds while keeping your feet planted and using the nod if you need to reset. Before we wrap up, does this updated plan feel like a realistic stretch, or does the prospect of staying twice as long feel daunting?

Sixty seconds sounds a bit scary, but not impossible. I think if I focus on the grounding first and remind myself it's just a loop, I could manage it. Maybe I'll set a quiet timer on my watch so I'm not just guessing. That way, I have a clear end point, and I can reward myself with a quick walk outside afterward.

That is a brilliant addition; using a visual timer removes the ambiguity of "when does it end?" and the promise of a fresh air break provides a natural incentive to stick with it. Combining the structural support of the timer, the safety net of the nod, and the motivation of the outdoor walk creates a robust framework for success. Just before we officially close, does having that concrete endpoint and reward make the sixty-second experiment feel significantly more achievable to you?

Hello again, and thank you for meeting with me today. To start, could you tell me a bit about how you spent the weekend and if there were any moments where you noticed yourself reacting differently to the dirty car? Also, on a scale of zero to ten, how would you rate your mood this morning compared to where we left off last time? Once we cover that, shall we briefly discuss what happened with the observation experiment you planned to try yesterday?

Hi. Well, the weekend was okay, I guess. I did notice myself getting tense every time I walked past the car, especially Saturday morning when the pollen was really bad. My mood this morning? Maybe a 5 or 6. It's been hovering around there. As for the experiment, I did try to just observe my thoughts without judging them, like you suggested. But honestly, I still felt that same sinking feeling.

It sounds like the sinking feeling persisted despite your intentional effort to just watch it pass, which can be incredibly frustrating when you know you're doing the right thing but the emotion remains stubborn. Let's explore that contrast a moment longer: when you successfully noted the tension rising in your chest versus when it felt like it took over completely, what was different about your internal narrative during those two instances?

Well, when I noticed it rising, I was telling myself, "Okay, here it comes again, just let it pass." But when it took over, my mind just jumped straight to "I'm a failure at keeping this car clean. People are probably looking at it and thinking I don't care." It's like that second voice is much louder and more convincing, you know?

That second voice about people judging you seems to amplify the initial shame, making the situation feel far more dangerous than it physically is. Have you ever caught yourself wondering why that specific thought—"people are looking"—seems so immediate and undeniable compared to the reality of who actually passed by?

I haven't really thought about that before. I mean, I don't actually see people staring or pointing. I just assume they're thinking it. When I really think about it, most folks are probably just focused on their own cars or their phones. But in that moment, it feels absolutely real, like everyone's attention is on my dirty car.

That gap between what you *know* is happening and what your brain *feels* is happening is exactly where the distortion lives. It seems like your mind automatically fills in the silence with worst-case scenarios because it's terrified of being judged. To test if that assumption holds water, could you recall a specific time recently when someone else drove by with a similarly dirty car, and what did you notice about their reaction—or lack thereof?

Hmm. Actually, just yesterday I saw a neighbor pull out with a white SUV that was absolutely covered in tree sap and dust. I remember thinking, "Wow, that's really bad," but I didn't judge them or think less of them. I just noticed it and went back to what I was doing. I didn't even give it a second thought until now. So I guess I don't assume the worst about them, but I assume everyone is doing that to me.

That comparison is powerful because it highlights the unfairness of holding yourself to a standard of invisibility that you clearly don't expect others to hold for themselves. It suggests your brain might be treating your car differently based on who owns it, rather than the actual level of mess. To dig deeper into that pattern, have you ever noticed if the intensity of that "everyone is judging" feeling changes depending on whether you're alone in the house or walking past neighbors?

You know, I think it does change. When I'm alone in the driveway and no one's around, the feeling isn't as sharp. I can look at the pollen and just sigh. But if I'm walking past neighbors or heading out to the car when people are outside, that's when the shame really kicks in. It's like their presence activates that loud voice in my head.

That distinction is fascinating because it reveals that the shame isn't just about the dirt itself, but about the perceived social exposure—the fear that others will witness your perceived inadequacy. It seems like your brain interprets anyone nearby as a potential critic, turning a private chore into a public performance you feel compelled to fail at. Before we finalize our next steps, could you rate how confident you feel that this new line of inquiry about audience perception will help reduce that panic tomorrow?

I'd say maybe a 6 or 7 out of 10. It does make sense logically that the panic is tied to having an audience, not just the dirt. But I'm still not sure how to stop that feeling in the moment when someone's actually walking by. I guess I need to practice reminding myself that they're probably not judging me the way I judge myself.

That insight about the audience being the catalyst is spot-on, and recognizing that panic spikes specifically when others are present gives us a precise target for our next experiment. Instead of trying to block out the feeling entirely—which often makes it louder—we can try a "social proof" trick: consciously recalling that neutral neighbor with the sap-covered SUV and mentally pairing their indifference with your current situation whenever someone walks by. Would you be willing to try this modified version tomorrow when you pass a neighbor, where you actively bring up that memory to counteract the judgment story?

Yeah, I think I can try that. It feels a bit strange to consciously call up that image of the dirty SUV when I'm feeling anxious, but I can see how it might help. I'll give it a shot tomorrow when I'm heading out and see if it takes the edge off that panic feeling. Maybe I'll even smile to myself about it.

That willingness to intentionally summon a calm memory to interrupt anxiety is a powerful form of mental rehearsal, and smiling adds a layer of self-compassion that softens the whole interaction. Before we lock this in, could you describe exactly what you'll do the first time you catch that panic rising near a neighbor? Should you stop walking, find a quiet spot to stand, or just pause for three seconds while bringing up the SUV image?

I think I'll just pause for a moment, maybe three seconds, right there on the path. I'll take a breath and picture that sap-covered SUV before I keep walking. That way I don't make a big production out of it, but I give myself a second to reset. I can also tell myself, "They're probably not even looking at my car," like a quick reminder.

That is a perfect, low-profile strategy because it keeps your behavior natural while inserting a gentle corrective thought right when the panic tries to hijack you. Since you've finalized the plan for tomorrow involving both the internal visualization and the external cue, how does having that specific "pause-and-reset" protocol sound feasible given your usual rush in the mornings? Is there anything else you'd like to adjust before we wrap up today?

It sounds feasible. I do tend to rush out in the mornings, but three seconds isn't going to make me late. I think I can manage that. No, I don't have anything else to adjust right now. I'll try it out and let you know how it goes next time. Thanks, this has been helpful.

That commitment to trying it out—even amidst the usual morning rush—is a fantastic sign of motivation and self-trust. I'm so glad we found a way to honor both your need for speed and your need for mental clarity. Before we officially close, could you share one word that best describes how this session made you feel? And is there anything about our work together that you wish we had touched on today?

Instantly, I thought, "My skin looks terrible—people must be staring at me." It was like my whole focus shifted from the music to that one thought, and I couldn't shake it for the rest of the walk.

That sudden shift from sensing the warmth to scanning for judgment highlights exactly why unstructured environments can be tricky—even with music playing, a quick glance can hijack your attention. It sounds like your brain latched onto that reflection as proof that the threat was real, overriding the safety of the music. Given that interruption, would you be open to adjusting our plan slightly? Instead of walking freely, could we try sitting in a park bench for ten minutes, keeping your headphones on, and consciously directing your gaze downward whenever you catch a fleeting image of yourself?

I guess I could try sitting on a bench instead. But honestly, just thinking about it makes me worry that I'll still catch a glimpse of my reflection in a puddle or someone's sunglasses. It feels like no matter where I go, there's always something to remind me of my sunburn and how bad it looks.

That is such a realistic hurdle—you are absolutely right that puddles and reflections are unavoidable reminders of your fear. It makes perfect sense that you'd anticipate failure before the trial begins. Let's adjust the plan to include a "contamination protocol": if you catch a glimpse in a puddle or window, simply acknowledge the sight silently ("There's water"), put your headphones back on immediately, and continue breathing until the urge passes. We won't judge the interruption; we'll just observe it and return to the music. Would you be willing to try this modified version tomorrow?

I think I can try that—just saying "there's water" or "there's a window" and then moving on. It feels a bit silly, but I guess the point is to stop myself from getting stuck on it. I'll give it a shot tomorrow afternoon and see how it goes.

That willingness to try the "label and return" method, even if it feels silly initially, shows great resilience. It turns a potentially overwhelming situation into a simple, manageable script you can follow. Before we lock this in, could you imagine sitting on that bench tomorrow with your headphones on, hearing that calm music, and noticing if your heart rate slows down once you successfully ignore the puddle? Does that visualization feel achievable to you right now?

Yeah, I can picture it—me on the bench with my music, and if I see a puddle, I just say "water" and look away. The part that feels hard is trusting that my heart rate will actually slow down. Usually, once I notice a reflection, my stomach drops and I feel tense for a while. But I guess the only way to find out is to actually try it and see if the script helps.

That honesty about trusting your physiology is crucial, and it shows you understand that the anxiety often lives in your body long after the initial thought passes. Let's frame this experiment as gathering data rather than proving a fact—if your heart stays elevated despite using the script, we'll learn together that the tension isn't permanent. Getting to the bench is indeed the biggest hurdle, but breaking it down shows you trust the process enough to take that first small leap. Before we officially close, could you tell me if there's anything else you want to reflect on about our session, or shall we wrap up here?
